interest: Documents US tracking of Canada's rapid shift toward expelling Japanese Canadians after Pearl Harbor, informing later US exclusion policy.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.20242H, File 1324), spanning December 1941 to January 1942, comprises diplomatic despatches, inter-agency transmittal memoranda, and contemporary newspaper clippings regarding the surveillance, demographic breakdown, property control, and impending removal of persons of Japanese ancestry in British Columbia following the outbreak of war between Canada and Japan. Authored primarily by Paul R. Josselyn, American Consul General in Vancouver, and addressed to the Secretary of State and American Minister Pierrepont Moffat in Ottawa, the documents record early wartime security measures enacted under the Defense of Canada Regulations. These include the RCMP's detailed registration of 23,428 Japanese residents, the closure of Japanese-language schools and newspapers, the impoundment and proposed liquidation of approximately 1,100 Japanese-operated fishing boats, the restriction and surveillance of the Japanese Consulate staff in Vancouver, and the comprehensive national policy statement issued by Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King on January 14, 1942, establishing coastal protected areas, civilian labor corps, and strict prohibitions on Japanese economic and navigational activities.
